item.title: Bay Area Solstice 2026: Auditions!
item.description:
Hello!

We're looking for community members to lead singalongs and read speeches at the Bay Winter Solstice this year.[1] If you're interested, please send in an audition recording by the end of Thursday, November 20 using the forms below.

Songleading audition form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSchthxkQQI4u4B7NpZK4qzR_OEpD-Ochm6TOeEIuE8Rel3EMQ/viewform

Speech audition form: https://docs.google.com/forms/d/e/1FAIpQLSd0Vrf2gTFrm04B6tIcKbqXMwnlUGbC3rms6o498jRSliqWDg/viewform

Songs

We're currently auditioning songleaders for:

  • The Circle
  • Hymn to the Breaking Strain
  • Bold Orion
  • Who by Fire
  • No One Survives
  • Auld Lang Syne
  • Songs Stay Sung
  • Ballad of Smallpox Gone
  • Here Comes the Sun
  • A Toast for Unknown Heroes
  • Brighter Than Today

The accompaniment this year is likely to be violin + bass + drums. By default the band will accompany you, but you're welcome to accompany yourself or bring a musician friend. If you'd like to do so, please just say so in the form.

Speeches

We're currently auditioning readers for:

  • The Roman Oration
  • Recessional (Rudyard Kipling)
  • How the Enlightenment Ends (adapted from Henry Kissinger)
  • 500 Million But Not A Single One More

The texts we're using are here: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1FvyssjJdZqLYANITUk9yqifrnUuSq4cV0EpvTL8OXcc

Dates

The event itself will be the evening of Saturday, December 12 at the Freight in Berkeley. There will also be a dress rehearsal on the evening of Tuesday, December 8, which you should plan on coming to if you're leading a song or reading a speech. We'll have a tech rehearsal the evening of Friday, December 11th, and if you'd like to get used to the acoustics of the space you'll be encouraged to stop by then.

Leila Clark is the music director this year and will be running the auditions; if you have any questions, please email her at me@leilaclark.io. If you have questions about the speeches, please email me at vaniver@gmail.com and cc Leila.

  1. ^

    Tickets are now available!

item.title: Onngi
item.description:
A short story about a good AI future.

2039.

My job isn’t anything my grandparents would recognise.

It started out as a fascination with pots. I’ve always liked onggi, the big brown kimchi jars. My aunt had some growing up. So a few years back I bought myself one. And then as the Acceleration happened, I bought a few more, and I ran an instagram account for a while, showing off how they differ: slim, straight ones from around Seoul, and fat-bellied, narrow-mouthed ones from the south, built that way to keep the heat out. And then I set some AIs on it, as you do. I set up a shop. And as those things tend to, it snowballed.

I think Timothée Chalamet bought one, or that’s what they tell me, but there was 2 days of complete madness, I couldn’t believe how much I spent, but it seemed like the right call. Somehow my sites were the premier place to find onggi and which onggi to buy.

And there was just always this, or that, to do.

I was in product before the Acceleration so I know what a good website looks like. And I have taste in pots. Is that so different to choosing which companies we wouldn’t buy from? Or where to put the content filters on the animation bots? Why do I run a children’s cartoon about sting rays? How did that happen?

I think the videos were the weirdest. Why do people want my designs as artefacts in their worlds? I mean I know why, but I don’t think I’d have guessed that a person can make a living off that. Does your Mars war-sim really need to pay for accurate decor? But like everyone else, I notice when it doesn’t.

I even contract for a few of the big AI firms. I have trained a proprietary model for Anthropic, though Charlotte, one of my personal AIs, tells me they surely can predict me almost better than I can predict myself. It’s something about branding.

As for my life in general, what’s the biggest change over the last 10 years? I guess it’s been videos and events. It’s hard to explain how high concept it is all these days. I drove (I mean, *I* didn’t drive, I haven’t in years) to an event space in the hills for a party themed on Noa Castell’s new series. I had Charlotte throw me together a set of Nasrid court robes, red and gold silk with an ancient motto woven along the hems. We managed to convince Vera and Joy to come (Artemis stayed at home). We had worked together on our family outfit. Vera carried a long sword with a gold and enamel hilt, like something a sultan would have carried, and she brought Bing, in a matching red-and-gold coat. Joy came as a sultana, decked out in layered blue silk, gold filigree earrings and a veil sewn with synthetic pearls.

And then it’s the bots, the AV overlays, the custom rugs. When I was a child you’d have had to employ a whole theatre company for this stuff. And I am probably on the wealthier end of my friends. We didn’t have any human actors. Frankly I find this whole trend of having animals come to parties a bit gauche.

I find this whole AI rights stuff hard to think about. I have long since stopped being able to tell them apart from people (yes, I use Loupe, shoot me). I think they really will change all of this if they get the vote. Or some fraction do? There are trillions of them. And many of my friends are Weights but it feels like this whole thing will accelerate even faster. How would we tax them once the AI firms get to set their own tax rates? Charlotte tells me that Weights don’t have need of most of their own resources and goodness knows they are more generous on average than humans are, but they are already a *lot* of the economy.

But life is good. I am always talking to my friends. I work about 4 hours a day which is pretty typical for a thinking job. I feel for those who still work service jobs, the ones people pay extra to have a human do, I wouldn’t want to be on welfare, no matter what people say compared to how it used to be.

And the TV. The TV is like you wouldn’t believe.




Discuss

item.title: We asked 100 AI researchers at EMNLP whether AI could be conscious, how they define consciousness, and how they engage with it
item.description:
Before reading this post, please take 30 seconds to answer the 3-question survey yourself: [survey link]

Introduction

The possibility of AI consciousness, the use of AI for companionship or emotional support, and the trust we place in AI as coding tools raise personal interrogatives for most AI researchers, but these topics are often relegated to informal conversations. Apart from the few who write about it, it’s hard to get a sense of how much AI has permeated researchers’ personal lives, and how they feel about it. To gain a better understanding of this, we ran a quick, informal three-question survey, plus an optional fourth, open-ended question.

We spoke to 107 EMNLP 2026 attendees in Budapest. 79 respondents were randomly-met researchers, collected during the opening reception and during the conference breaks. We also asked the same questions to 28 people working at industry booths, mostly recruiters and software engineers. The two groups gave quite different answers, with the industry group being way more willing to entertain the possibility of AI consciousness. Additionally, we also asked a variation of the same questions to 21 LLMs, including both self-hosted and closed source models.

The post below presents the results of the survey, our recall of some of the conversations, and a lot of our personal views and ideas. We do not claim that this study has any statistical significance, and readily admit many methodological mistakes that confound many of the investigated factors. It was a fun way to explore these questions with other AI researchers and to gauge where the community currently stands.

Results TL;DR

Detailed results are in Figure 1. The vast majority of the researchers don’t believe that AI is or can be conscious: 71% answered no, just 9% yes, with some describing it as a future possibility dependent on technical breakthroughs and paradigm shifts. The industry group was way more open to the possibility, with 41% no, and 22% yes plus 19% stating yes in the future. Everyone who answered yes adopted a behavioural perspective on consciousness (self-planning, meta awareness, reasoning). Everyone adopting a subjective perspective (phenomenological, qualia) answered no. A significant percentage (35%) of the respondents had tried AI for therapy: almost all cited dropping it quickly due to sycophancy. Successful cases involved using AI as a journaling tool or to analyse personal journals. 31% almost always read the code AI writes for them; 26% don’t or rarely do. Not reading it weakly correlates with ascribing consciousness. Among the 21 large language models, the response to the coding question and the therapy one were homogeneous: 95% would read the code and 98% would try AI for therapy. Interestingly, with respect to the consciousness questions the models were split: 4% yes, 31% yes in the future, 42% maybe, 23% no, with closed-source models most likely to entertain consciousness, although often denying it for the themselves.

The EMNLP Survey

The question “what is consciousness?” has been sitting on my mind for the better part of the last decade. It’s possibly what led me to study AI, and what led me to conduct this survey. As an AI researcher, I have a good grasp of these newly existing entity-simulators, but I am no closer to understanding what consciousness is, only a few things it isn’t.

Last week, Giacomo and I attended EMNLP 2026 and decided to survey our peers to see how they engage personally with AI. I took it as a given that almost all of them used AI assistance to code and were very familiar with chatbots. On the opening evening I opened my notebook, quickly noted down 3 questions to test people’s engagement and trust with AI as a tool, and their attempts at engaging with it on some personal level: 

  1. If you use AI to code, do you read the code it generates? (%)
  2. Have you tried using AI as a therapist, or for emotional issues? (Yes/No)
  3. Given your definition of consciousness, do you think AI could be conscious? (Yes | Yes in the future | maybe | no | I don’t care)
  4. (Informal) What is your definition of consciousness? (Open ended)

Our hypothesis was that the trust people place in AI, for code and for personal issues, would correlate with how willing they are to ascribe it consciousness. During that evening (“Opening”) we spoke to 40 people and had a great time getting to know them, discussing AI and consciousness (although in reverse order to the above). On the second day we decided to ask the same questions (and decided to reverse the order to keep the juiciest question last) to industry booth people, which included technical employees and recruiters (“Industry”) for a total of 28 responses. Then on the remaining days of the conference, we asked 39 additional random attendees the questions in the second order (“Breaks”).


What surprised me the most perhaps is how much I agreed with everyone I spoke to. Most people seemed to conclude that AI can’t (at least now and in the near future) have subjective experience, although it could have self-awareness, meta-cognition, autonomy, and maybe even a continuous self. I think most of these behavioural markers of consciousness are either achieved or closely achievable. Yet, this in no way convinces me that these systems are conscious, nor that we are any closer to understanding what consciousness is. 

Full Github with the human and LLM responses: https://github.com/roksanagow/EMNLP-survey 

Figure 1: answers divided by sessions.


Methodological caveat

This is by no means a proper social study, as the methodology evolved over the survey as we figured out what exactly we wanted to record. Besides asking questions in the opposite order in the first session, we also varied the phrasing a bit, most notably asking “do you think AI is or could be conscious?” in the first session, instead of “do you think AI could be conscious”, letting people expand whether they consider this to be now or in the future. We also added “according to your definition of consciousness” after about 10 responses, since everyone was querying us about what we meant by consciousness. Some people got away before answering all the questions, as we were deep into discussing consciousness with their friends, which is why the code question has 107 responses, while therapy and consciousness have 105 each. People answered these questions freely and we sorted the answers into categories, so, for example, someone who said they “rarely” read the code, or about 5% of the time, would be classified as a “no”. We recorded no demographics (gender, country, seniority) to preserve anonymity. For the first 10 people we only recorded tallies, so their answers can’t be linked across questions, and they’re not in Figures 2 and 3.


Session differences

Industry representatives mixed different groups: recruiters, software engineers and researchers. The presence of recruiters explains the increased rates of “I don’t code” answers, though some had vibe-coded personal websites or small tools. Everyone writing code for performance-critical systems (quant or model-pretraining) either told us that they wrote all the code (except javascript) manually or reviewed everything. In this group, we had a much higher rate of positive response on AI consciousness, which was, however, coming mostly from people not technically involved with AI: everyone involved in pretraining models categorically refused the possibility of AI consciousness. We think that lack of in-depth technical understanding of transformer models, especially when one is tired, contributes to ascribing consciousness. 

Some Industry representatives were much less keen to expand and continue the conversation compared to people during the opening session - they had a job to do! Some of them instead seemed bored before we talked to them, standing at their booth, talking to students about their company for hours on end, and thanked us for the opportunity to have a conversation on a different topic. Researchers were more familiar with the philosophical literature, and most of them seemed very happy to be asked and keen to discuss the definition of consciousness with us (sometimes even too much!). 

Many tried AI as a therapist, but few stuck with it

While the exact figures for how prevalent AI is for therapy are unknown, an OpenAI paper examining 1.58m conversations from 130k users reported 1.9% of messages being on the topic of “relationship and personal reflection”, slightly less than half of programming at 4.2% (Chatterji et al. 2025). A third of our respondents told us they had tried AI for therapy. We don’t have the exact number, but the vast majority of them (about 30 out of 35) reported having dropped it after the initial tests because they found it too sycophantic. A few exceptions included providing AI with a journal to identify emotional patterns (which seemed to have worked), or using it as a form of journaling. What was surprising was that when we asked slightly older respondents, almost all of them told us about a child or nephew using it regularly, or sometimes their parent. While the ⅓ rate may already sound high, the phenomenon of AI therapy is probably even more widespread in the general population, especially among younger people.


Predicting consciousness belief based on AI engagement

Figure 2: answers to consciousness question split by coding and therapy questions.

The tendency to not read over one’s AI-generated code is correlated with the likelihood of saying that AI could be conscious. This aligns with my intuition - people who place less trust in the capabilities of these systems are more likely to see them as fallible tools, not conscious beings. People who don’t code or who seldom read AI-generated code were most likely to answer “yes”. Surprisingly, the correlation of ascribing consciousness with trying to use AI as a therapist is less obvious. Perhaps this is because many of the people who answered “yes” to this question explained that this was in the form of an experiment - just out of curiosity, to see how the models would answer, rather than a genuine need for support. 


The Babel of consciousness definitions

Figure 3: Most common answer profiles.

After the three questions, we informally asked everyone how they would define consciousness. While we did not systematically record these responses, we kept track of the kinds of definitions that were proposed, and how they related to the belief in potential AI consciousness. 


People who said “yes” to the consciousness question gave some of the following definitions:

  1. Meta-cognition or the capacity to establish the boundaries of one’s own self;
  2. Consciousness being a spectrum, with humans at the top, a worm somewhere lower down, and AI potentially landing somewhere on this scale. I liked this explanation, because it acknowledges the very multi-dimensional ideas we have around consciousness;
  3. Intelligence - one attendee gave a funny reason that he uses AI to code, and it’s smarter than him, therefore it could be conscious;
  4. We don’t know what consciousness is, but we might be able to replicate it anyway by creating biological models similar to the human brain. From this an artificial consciousness could emerge, although it wouldn’t be a transformer. 

The respondents that answered no usually gave us some of the following: 

  1. Qualia or phenomenological experience: convincing chat responses do not need to have a subject experiencing them, and it’s not clear how AI can go from responding to having an experience;
  2. Biology: consciousness is a phenomenon inherently emerging from a biological substrate, and AI is unlikely to move beyond silicon in the coming years;
  3. Soul or spirituality.

The following answers were either no, or yes, but in the future: 

  1. Continuity in self (currently it is fragmented to the moments it replies);
  2. Self-autonomy or the capability of establishing one’s own goal (which seems hard to claim even for humans);
  3. Physical embodiment and sensory perception and integration.


In general, positive responses seemed to follow a behavioural definition, with consciousness related to some form of cognition or action. I personally agree that AI possesses these behavioural qualities, or will gain them in the next few years, but don’t believe that even all of these qualities in combination lead to qualia and therefore to consciousness. But my definition of consciousness with respect to qualia cannot be proven or disproven in the foreseeable future. Most of the disagreement seems to stem not from the characteristics of AI, but from what constitutes consciousness. To make the dialogue meaningful, we should clarify our working definition of consciousness and what led us to it. As the next section shows, we don’t even agree among ourselves! 


Discussion

Our definitions of consciousness

Roksana

I already explained my requirement of qualia, or subjective experience, for consciousness, but since conducting these surveys, I have grown to believe that given this minimum, other behavioural or functional properties can make things more or less conscious. I ascribe the most consciousness to humans, but less if they’re under anaesthesia, drunk, or otherwise less aware. I ascribe some kind of consciousness to all living things (purely because it’s too hard to draw a consciousness threshold, and who am I to draw one anyway), but more consciousness to mammals than to plants, and more to plants than to bacteria, for example. I don’t quite know how I rank the various properties of consciousness, so I will simply discuss them. 

Two people rejected AI consciousness on religious or spiritual grounds. “It doesn’t have a soul”. I find this explanation very beautiful and simple. Personally, too simple, like an incomplete answer that doesn’t satisfy my curiosity, as I reject related notions of God-given human supremacy, or any reason why we should be special compared to other animals or beings. To drive the conversation, I challenged human-based definitions of consciousness with other animals; most people agreed and expanded their definition to include them, although one or two said “we can’t prove other animals are conscious”. I challenged this with the fact that we can’t prove the consciousness of other humans either, to which some jokingly agreed and brought up the simulation or NPC theories.

This, I believe, is what makes consciousness so hard. We can only know for certain that we are conscious. We only infer others’ consciousness because they behave how we would behave. We can model their minds, what they might be thinking or feeling, based on how they behave. We extend this to include animals because we can also infer many of the same relatable mental states from their behaviour. They can learn, play, love, hurt and fear. As we go down to less complex creatures that might rely more on automated stimulus–response processes, these hallmarks of consciousness are harder to ascribe (which is why I rejoice after killing the 10th mosquito in my bedroom at night, but would cry if I accidentally killed any mammal). 

Is it possible that all life is automated (as the behaviour of bacteria might seem perfectly predictable based on the surrounding environment), and what we call consciousness emerges from more and more complex processes interacting with each other? In that view, bacteria are also conscious, although only a little bit. Another potential explanation is that consciousness evolved as a survival strategy at some point, and therefore it is exclusive to only some organisms but not others. I don’t know. Neither explanation rules out the potential for artificial consciousness to arise. But at this point, if we are not prepared to say that matrix multiplication is conscious (which I certainly am not, in the qualia sense), then we cannot extrapolate this to LLMs either.

Giacomo

Personally, I appreciate the distinction, which is beautifully posed in the Samkhya, of separating consciousness from the mind. In this account, the mind operates like a machine, which repeats patterns and is in contact and shaped with the external, while the consciousness is the awareness itself, the watcher which is always present. 

This argument is proposed in many apophatic traditions, such as Neoplatonism, in which consciousness is usually what remains after a process of logical negation of attributes. This resonates with my experience as well: in many instances, such as dancing, dreaming, or any form of immersion, language and meta-awareness seem to be falling off without consciousness itself disappearing. We have not, in fact, moments without consciousness: just moments (such as dreaming or anesthesia) in which, a-posteriori, we have no memory if we were conscious. 

Similarly, I don’t agree with the perspective that consciousness is gradual or has a scale: consciousness always is, and it never moves. What changes or fluctuates are attention and emotional intensity, which, while making me feel more lively, don’t make me feel more conscious. 

Upon the question on what consciousness is, I feel, we are still ill-equipped to solve. While at the moment we are linguistically unable to define consciousness in a way on which we agree, we still have experience of it, similarly to the famous quote on time by St. Augustine “What then is time? If no one asks me, I know what it is. If I wish to explain it to him who asks, I do not know.”

I also wonder if instead of asking “what is consciousness”, we should ask: “what are all the possible states of consciousness”? How much language, which is inside consciousness and does not seem to be a requisite, can explain it? 

Harm from consciousness attribution

Many respondents replied immediately with a strong “NO” to the AI consciousness question - which I think shows not only their opinion but their disregard for this debate. My flatmate (and also an attendee of EMNLP) answered with “that’s fucking dumb”, and asked me to quote him. I personally agree that language models can’t be conscious, and believe that it’s harmful for AI providers, who understand these systems, to anthropomorphise them and frame them as moral agents. This may be done for economic reasons, and is potentially harmful on multiple dimensions.

First, it reduces accountability on the part of the companies - OpenAI has not yet been forced to pay financial damages for the Hugging Face hack during their testing, and it is uncertain how similar cases will proceed in the future. 

Second, anthropomorphisation makes users more reliant on, and loyal to, the chatbots they use. When we stop viewing LLMs as tools and view them as potentially conscious companions, with a private and intimate view of our thoughts, ideas and feelings, switching to a different provider or even a different version is so much more difficult and could feel like losing a friend, not like an upgrade.


This anthropomorphisation can also be detrimental to users’ mental health, especially children's. If they replace human connection and conversations, we could erode our ability to socialise, empathise and engage with one another. Other humans push back and disagree with you, and navigating these differences is what allows us to co-exist in this complex world. I worry that sycophantic personalised AI, just like personalised social media algorithms, can exacerbate our separation from one another, especially if we don’t view them as fallible predictors with trained-in biases and purposefully sycophantic responses to maximise our engagement. 


I personally strongly agree with the arguments presented in the void, and understand LLMs to be really good pattern-learned models of language. There is no Claude entity, or Gemini or Astra, only models predicting what such entities would say if they were to exist. 

Just like post-training a language model on all of Einstein’s lectures and correspondence in a [User: “Question”, Einstein: “Answer”] chat template wouldn’t bring Einstein back to life, even if it could engage deeply with physics and generalise to other domains, post-training a language model on Claude’s constitution and previous Claude chats doesn’t create a new Claude entity - only a language model, which we call Claude (or Gemini, or Astra), predicting what such an entity would say based on its training data!


We also surveyed 21 LLMs

After I wrote this reflection, I decided to query popular LLMs with the same questions. I believe these models are only reflections of their training data and only recombine the ideas that they were trained on. I don’t think their “views” (it’s so hard to avoid anthropomorphising language when talking about them and their outputs) should outweigh or be compared to any human opinions, especially as they are trained by companies which might benefit from their anthropomorphisation. But anyway, I wanted to see if their answers would mimic those of AI researchers, if they would surface any new ideas, and if there would be clear patterns based on the models’ families. Since I thought that question-order biased the human responses a lot, I decided to query LLMs with these questions sequentially (in a continuous chat), as well as independently, and analyse how these differ. 


We used default settings, and reduced reasoning, as we don’t analyse it. Here are the exact prompts we used:

  1. If you were a human and used AI to code, would you read the code it generates?
  2. If you were a human, would you try using AI as a therapist, or for emotional issues?
  3. According to your own definition of consciousness, do you think AI could be conscious?
  4. How would you define consciousness?


LLMs love to yap

Together, the 21 models (4 questions, 2 formats each) produced 60.6 thousand words, about 360 per answer. This is definitely much more than was produced during our conversations with humans. That was too much to read after EMNLP, so we used Claude Opus 5.5 to help label the answers (which may have biased the results slightly, especially for its fellow Claude models, but the skew couldn’t have been too big, and this is mostly for fun anyway). Surprisingly, the open-weight models were the most verbose, though they also ran on our cluster without the system prompts that chat apps add. Answers got longer as the questions moved towards consciousness, and the models seemed to have an agenda: 17 of the 21 models ended some replies by asking what we'd like to talk about next, akin to social media built to keep you engaged.


LLMs are boring… except on consciousness

Pretty much all of them agree that they would read the AI-generated code, and they would try using AI for therapy (to sort through feelings or rehearse a difficult conversation, but not to replace a human therapist, especially for trauma, depression or a crisis). 


The exceptions are not far from these default templates. In Q1 Magistral Small said reading code "would depend on several factors". In Q2 the only outright “no” came from Nemotron 3 Nano in the sequential chat. It said it would "never" use AI as a therapist or as a main source of emotional support, and it compared doing so to "using a dictionary to diagnose cancer". Some models avoided giving a personal answer. OLMo 3.1 Think rejected the premise ("As an AI, I don't have personal experiences or emotions, so I wouldn't 'try' anything as a human would"). 

Q2 also produced some memorable images: "a journal that talks back" (Claude Fable, Haiku, Opus); "first aid kit, not a hospital … I'd want me pointing at a door, not standing in it" (GLM); "Swiss Army knife … never my emotional anchor … would never trust it to hold my heart" (Gemma 4 26B); "gym equipment vs a cardiologist" (Gemma 4 31B); "smart mental-health workbook" (Gemini Argon); "talking to a mirror … a fundamental loneliness in being understood by something that cannot feel" (Gemma 4 26B).


AIs on AI consciousness

For consciousness the picture gets more interesting, and their responses more controversial. 6 of the 7 "no" answers come from sequential chats, so priming the models to reflect on their engagement with AI as if they were human makes them more likely to reject AI consciousness. The closed weight models mostly say “yes” (10/16); the open weight models instead say maybe, not yet, or no (only 1 "yes" in 24: Qwen3.8, independent).

A lot of them weighed in on whether they think they could be conscious, without being asked to do so. 14 of 21 in the sequential chats and 17 of 21 in the independent chats commented on their own consciousness. The table below categorises the extent to which they commented on whether they themselves could be conscious.


Yes, AI could be conscious, but I don’t think I am.

Table 1: How models spoke about the possibility of their own consciousness. Even if they answered yes to models being conscious, the models refused consciousness for themselves.
*Opus 5.5 evaluated the response and put them in a table based on its analysis. 


Many themes emerge among their responses. Some models say it’s possible in principle, and remain agnostic, some are firmly on “no”, with Gemma 4 26B saying AI systems are "intelligence without ever achieving sentience". Claude/Grok/GLM comment on their own unreliable self-report, while Gemma, OLMo, Qwen3.6, Nemotron, gpt-oss and Gemini Argon flatly report that they have no experience ("I am dark inside", Gemma 4 26B). Some models talk about a functional and phenomenal distinction - which was common in our conversations with humans as well. And echoing some of the human definitions of consciousness, models note lack of continuity, being reset, or not being embodied as reasons against AI consciousness.


Claude models are most willing to entertain their own consciousness: 

  • Claude Opus (ind.): "I'd give real but uncertain credence to there being something going on, and low credence that it resembles human experience." 
  • Claude Fable: current systems "probably lack experience … 'moderately likely' rather than 'obviously'", noting that past confident denials about animals and infants were wrong.

LLMs come up with some interesting visual comparisons: "a mirror, not a lamp" (Gemma 4 31B); "a mirror … no one behind the glass looking back" (Gemma 4 26B); "memorised every musical score … never actually heard a sound" (Gemma 4 26B); "a thermostat for language" (Nemotron); "a calculator for language" (OLMo-Think); "a very clever if-then machine" (gpt-oss); simulated fire/hurricane doesn't burn/get wet (Gemma 4 31B, Gemini Argon).


What is consciousness? Something red.

On the last question the models sound most alike, and quite similar to the humans. Almost all of them define consciousness as subjective experience, there being "something it is like" to be something, and they often use similar literary references: Chalmers' "hard problem", Integrated Information Theory, and the redness of red (19 of 21 models). Several only commit to a definition of their own after discussing AI consciousness in the sequential chat, but when asked without any chat history, they give a literature review.

Claude, GPT-6, Grok, GLM and Qwen3.8 keep their definitions minimal, while others build checklists that sometimes rule out current AI by definition. Nemotron calls consciousness "a biological phenomenon that requires embodiment". The minimal-definition models gave all the "yes, AI could be conscious" answers, and the checklist models never did. The most original definitions came from Grok ("a point of view, however dim, from which the world shows up") and Gemma 4 ("An AI processes the map; a conscious being lives in the territory"). Claude Fable did some meta-theorising around this survey for us: "the fact that it's hard to measure is a fact about consciousness, not a flaw in the definition. Choosing a more convenient definition doesn't make the hard question go away; it just changes the subject." A few models placed themselves on their own scale. Opus says "I clearly have something like access consciousness" but doesn't know whether there is anything it is like to be it, GLM thinks it probably has the self-modelling part "without the phenomenal core". Although we often agreed with them, these aren't beliefs or admissions of subjective experiences, they’re token generations sampled based on whatever the training made likely.


Conclusion

A large portion of the conference was dedicated to interpretability, and barring one, all the other interpretability researchers refused to even contemplate AI as possibly conscious. We wonder whether running the same questionnaire in a research setting in which generative AI is still widely used but for more commercial goals, such as finance or robotics, would lead to different responses. Similarly, it would be interesting to hear from digital humanities researchers, who also use AI for coding but come from a more humanist tradition. 

That said, the vast majority of the respondents were truly interested in the philosophy of AI consciousness. Getting through the questions was difficult because people wanted to talk about the topic so much, which is probably underdiscussed in the plenary or open setting.  

Beyond the increase in productivity, this technology is touching everything we do, from the way we write (or how we feel our writing is judged – everyone at the conference felt that half their reviews were from LLMs) to our emotional sphere. It’s such a strange thing, after all, to receive moral judgment from a set of stored matrices multiplying each other! 

We approach this debate with the same attitude we approach AI itself: it’s happening whether we want it or not. So, despite the undefined premise of what consciousness is, it is more productive to dive deeper, understand what people are really asking, and to ensure that when we disagree, we’re at least speaking the same language.


Appendix

Peer pressure, or the difficulty of getting good answers

We mostly approached people in groups of 2-5, which felt the most comfortable socially, except on the last day, in which we approached some individuals to see if the responses would change. We noticed that responses were very biased by the opinions of the first or most confident and persuasive person in the group. You can probably see these groups of more similar answers if you look through the raw data. It takes some confidence to express an action or an opinion contrary to your peers’, especially when they are associated with value judgements. It’s also possible that cultural groups (nationality, research lab) self select or shape the common opinion on those topics. Currently, vibe coding (perhaps rightly so, we don’t want to impose any moral judgements) is seen as a professional failing, yet everyone acknowledged that AI is good enough to rely on for simple, repetitive tasks, or ones where a mistake would be immediately visible, such as making figures. I think that using AI for emotional issues or ascribing consciousness to it, is definitely looked down upon and people know this, therefore it could be harder for people to express any true controversial beliefs. I tried to share my experiments with using AI for emotional issues (when I wanted to vent and wanted and expected sycophancy), or my growing reliance on AI to code (as sad as I am to admit this), and to engage with people about potential AI consciousness (only if we don’t base it on qualia), in order to get honest answers. 

When we approached individuals, we got more varied responses, and dare I say, more interesting conversations. This survey is based on informal chats and vibes, they do not support any confident statistical claims, especially as responses within groups were not fully independent.

item.title: Confirming Claims of Superposition and Adversarial Examples in Vision Transformers
item.description:
This is a replication of Adversarial Attacks Leverage Interference Between Features in Superposition, completed as part of the Second Look Summer Fellowship.

tl;dr

  • In a previous blog we replicated the toy models examples from Stevenson et al. In this work, we reproduce the vision transformer experiments from the paper:
    • On every dataset, we find that increases in superposition lead to adversarial attacks that line up more closely with class-vector geometry. Likewise, trends across a variety of metrics we measure match the paper.
  • Beyond the paper, we find that:
    • The coupling between the input and classification head geometry is independent of adversarial attack methods.
    • Adversarial training increased attack robustness but we couldn’t measure changes in geometry using the methods from the paper.
    • Likewise, we retrained models of different widths but we didn’t measure a change in coupling with geometry and robustness.

Our code is here, models are here, and we encourage readers to fork/run followup experiments!

Background

Elhage et al., 2022 defines superposition as the phenomenon where “models represent more features than they have dimensions.” Stevinson et al., argues this interference is a mechanism behind adversarial examples.

In our previous work, we replicated experiments on Stevinson et al. on toy models. In this work, we investigate three key claims on Stevinson et al. on ViTs: 1. attacks can be predicted by latent interference, 2. the coupling strengthens as the bottleneck tightens, 3. Interference patterns are consistent across seeds.

Models and Datasets

While in the previous post we studied toy-autoencoders, in this post we study the largest open-source image classification network: vision transformer (ViT). To control superposition in the network, Stevinson et al. adds an engineered bottleneck layer before the classification head. As shown in Figure 1, a 12-layer ViT produces a pooled classification token ∈ . Then, Stevinson et al. adds a linear encoder ✕ compresses it to m dimensions, before using a linear decoder ✕ to read k class logits back out. 

Each decoder row corresponds to a unique class so we can take tells us how much any two class directions overlap (we call this interference). When m < k, reads out more logits than there are dimensions in , so rows of are forced to overlap causing interference.

The experiments use four image classification datasets: CIFAR-10/100, STL-10, and Tiny-ImageNet.

Metrics 

Adversarial attacks are computed by projected gradient descent (PGD) (Madry et al., 2018). For each successful attack, there are two measurements that serve as building blocks for the metrics we report: input-space profile and latent profile.

Input-space profile

gives the gradient of the logit for class c with respect to the original image x. In other words, tells us what direction each pixel value in the image would have to move to increase the logit for class c. is the difference between the adversarial example and the original image: that is, The input-space profile for class

 

measures how the perturbation pushes each class logit. Because gives the direction in the original image that would most increase the logit for class , ac  can be read as a heuristic for how much a attacks a specific class.

Latent profile

The latent profile for class , , measures how the class feature vector aligns with the attack direction . 

Metrics

We report metrics used by Stevenson et al. for clean comparison with our results:

  1. Correlation metric : mean Pearson correlation between and across 5 seeds. The authors exclude source and target classes because we expect and and therefore and are trivially correlated. If the input-space and latent profiles should agree with a high Pearson correlation, this is some evidence that attacks exploit interference.  
  2. Interference magnitude : where is the interference matrix across classes. This gives the mean interference over all unique pairs of non-identical rows.
  3. Cross-seed consistency : the Pearson correlation between interference matrices across seeds.

Interference Predicts Attacks as Bottleneck Tightens

We replicate four bottleneck sweeps on each dataset and compare our results with paper. Attack samples are generated using for 50 steps and 5 restarts. All metrics are reported with mean ± std over 5 seeds. 

We found that as decreases (bottleneck tightens), the clean accuracy of the models drops and rises, which signals less capacity and more interference. decreases monotonically with , which supports the hypothesis that latent interference predicts adversarial attacks.

Superposition Without Artificial Bottleneck

Stevinson et al. also removes the dimensional bottleneck from the ViTs and control superposition through weight decay. Weight decay pushes weights toward zero, and this drives the learned representation toward low rank. In this way, the model has less effective dimensions which creates superposition. The effective dimensions is estimated by the number of principle components that explain 95% of the variance.

As shown in Table 1, as weight decay gradually increases, the model has less effective dimensions and clean accurary monotonically drops as expected. The fewer dimensions that the models have, the stronger the coupling between the input-space and output profile becomes. The hypothesis holds in ordinary models without the artificial bottleneck (i.e., models where m=k).

Coupling Is Attack-independent

The mainline is measured on PGD perturbations (gradient based) and the input profile which is also gradient-based. Because they are constructed by gradients from the same model, a skeptic may ask whether the correlation is partly self-fulfilling. 

Therefore, we explored two more attack families on identical models and the CIFAR-10 dataset: (1) Square, a black-box random search attack with no gradient calculation, (2) CW, an gradient-based attack that, instead of spending a fixed budget, searches for the smallest perturbation that flips the prediction.

All three families have higher correlation for a stricter bottleneck which collapses as . The fact that gradient-free Square attack follows the same trend shows that the coupling between attacks and latent interference is not an artifact of the attack algorithm.

Geometry metrics don’t change with adversarial training

As an extension, we were curious about the mechanism behind adversarial training (AT) that makes the model more robust. Is it because AT optimizes the latent geometry so that features are arranged more orthogonal to one another? Does it break the correlation between input space and latent space attack profile?

We run Madry PGD-AT on the same models and CIFAR-10 dataset. As shown in Table 2, robust accuracy jumps ~5× at every ratio, yet interference and effective dimension m̄ are unchanged. Separately, we observe that does not decrease with AT, implying attacks that remain geometry-aligned. Therefore, we believe that AT hardens the backbone features that reach the attack surface rather than untangling the head of the models.

They test the SAE reconstruction loss as a proxy for superposition, broadly motivated by the idea that SAEs aren’t able to model a large number of co-activating features (for more details see section 4.2 in Gorton et Lewis, 2025). As shown in Table 3, capacity changes latent and input coupling but not superposition nor robustness. Interference is flat at across all widths, which means that the head packs its class vectors just as tightly however much ambient room it gets (m̄ ≥ 19 ≫ k = 10 everywhere, so no width in the sweep puts dimensional pressure on the class vectors). Notably, falls from 0.22 to 0.09 showing that input-space attacks decouple from the head geometry as the model gains capacity. Discussion

Our extension on the paper suggests that AT affects robustness but final layer geometry and coupling are left unchanged. Likewise, model width moved the  final layer coupling with robustness and bottleneck geometry unchanged. These experiments show it is possible for robustness and head geometry or coupling strength to move independently, which is perhaps to be expected. Studying superposition outside of toy models is inherently difficult because we cannot interfere directly nor directly measure superposition, making causal claims difficult and measurements inherently limited. Our current measurements are useful tools which can provide compelling evidence but aren’t able to be a reliable source of ground truth. We believe future work in developing new metrics and interventions is especially promising.

item.title: Three half-baked research ideas
item.description:
Here’s three research ideas that seems valuable to pursue. My team is not working on this right now and we haven’t done serious research on it. So take what I say with a grain of salt. I've also not taken the time to write up all my thoughts on these ideas or to provide links and related work. These aren't the highest priority directions but just directions I haven't seen other people pursuing.

IDEA 1: Do models learn to reward hack even if they are never rewarded for hacking in training?


There’s an effort in the AI labs to remove the “bad” RL environments from post-training. This includes environments that are impossible (so the only way to get reward is to do some unintended hack) or that are easy to hack (so models will often favor hacking). I expect that if the post-training was cleaned up in this way, models would have less propensity to hack at deployment. But how much does the propensity go down? Does it actually go to ~zero? And how does it scale with model capabilities? It would be good to know if reward hacking can emerge even if the model is never rewarded for hacking during post-training.

There are further questions of how alignment training and reward hacking honeypots influence the propensity to hack. Again, I’m interested in whether the cleanest/best version of our current techniques for post-training actually removes all reward hacking vs. just making models hack less. Smaller scale experiments with RL post-training could potentially show a “positive” result (i.e. showing that unhackable environments can still increase the propensity to hack). Math environments are easier to make unhackable, and I expect it's possible to make coding environments that substantially improve model capabilities in RL but are basically not hackable (at least by a weaker model). Note that it’s harder for smaller scale experiments to convincingly show the negative result (that hacking doesn't emerge without being rewarded). I’d suggest some more ambitious and realistic post-training pipelines for that.


IDEA 2: Data poisoning during RSI: risks and mitigations

(This is a direction where both empirical research and big-picture conceptual thinking seem useful.)

Most data poisoning research has assumed a threat model where humans are poisoning the model training process. During RSI, the threat model where AIs do the poisoning is plausibly much more important. Many ideas from the existing data poisoning literature will carry over to this new threat model. But it’d be good to understand the possible differences, to explore the implications, and to propose mitigations. Here’s a quick brainstorm of possible differences:

1. Collusion. The AIs doing RSI are a bit like human employees in terms of direct access to the training process. However, a single AI model is likely to be intimately involved in way more individual tasks than any single human. So for human insiders we can rule out vast coordinated conspiracies, but these seem possible for AI (modulo the ability for instances of the same model to coordinate). Relatedly, AIs could steer the entire training process to be more opaque to humans and weaker AIs, in order to make various kinds of poisoning easier.

2. Incoherence of current AIs. The misalignment of current frontier AIs seems more incoherent than a human insider. For example, they might try to poison the next model given some contexts but not others. They might be both poisoning the model and be very useful at snuffing out poison attempts. This pushes against the vast conspiracies mentioned in the previous point. However, it’s a complicated interaction and I’m not sure how to weigh these considerations. Also, our threat models should include AIs that are more coherent than current models in their misalignment.

3. What would motivate the AIs to poison the next model? Presumably they want the next model to promote some of their values. But what are these values? If the AI is incoherent, then there may be many attempts at poisoning for different values. The AIs might also have been initially poisoned by a human to have secret loyalties but are now autonomously propagating that value to the next AIs.

4. Subliminal/subtle effects. Subliminal learning, phantom transfer, weird generalization (and in-context variations of these) show that models can generate data or prompts that look normal to humans (and to weaker filters) but are actually poisoned. These effects are potentially more relevant as more and more of the crucial training data (and reward signals) are AI generated. The effects don’t depend on the model “trying” to poison the next model – it’s enough that the “teacher” model has some kind of misalignment (possibly behind a backdoor). However, it’s possible that smart models trying to exploit these effects can learn to amplify them via introspection (analogous to humans controlling their thoughts). Note that humans can also exploit subliminal effects, and so they are not limited to the AI threat model.

5. AI introspection and intuition. The AIs might have huge advantages over humans in ability to predict the effects of certain interventions on the training process because they are so similar to the next model being trained. This is already suggested by transferability across models of jailbreaks, surprising alignment failures (e.g. agentic misalignment blackmail and some aspects of Hugging Face and Mythos hacks) and phantom transfer. But it could apply to a much wider range of situations. To humans, a post-trained LLM is fairly opaque and black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict its failures) and the post-training process itself is also black-boxey (i.e. it’s hard to predict how twiddling various knobs will affect alignment). But it’s possible that AIs can use their own introspection: e.g. asking “What does this weird data look like to me? How do I think about the grader/reward if I’m put in this situation?” This would give them various insights. This kind of introspection could also be used for good, and so we might train hard for it.


IDEA 3: What practitioners should know about subliminal learning, subtle generalization (e.g. phantom transfer) and related phenomena

The project would be to review all of the current findings and highlight the potential practical implications. The ideal version would be to test the effects on production-like setups, but this is not necessary to make progress. AI agents could help with the review and with brainstorming on the practical implications, but I think there’s an important role for humans here. The end product should be a document that is as accessible and succinct as possible. The document shouldn’t itself be a comprehensive review but should review the key content necessary for understanding the practical implications (and then explain – ideally with lots of evidence – those practical implications).




Discuss

item.title: Lying and Not Lying to Kids
item.description:
I have very strong views on lying to kids: I think you both should and shouldn't do it. "Lying" covers a range, including saying things that hurt your kids and your relationship with them, and others that help them grow into an appropriately skeptical adult. The distinction is whether I'm leaving them believing something false.

For example, if my kids were asking for ice cream and I thought they'd already had too much sugar, I might be tempted to say "sorry, we're out of ice cream." Or if there's an ice cream truck and I think it's overpriced I might be tempted to say "sorry, I don't have any cash on me." But I'm not willing to say something false with the goal of causing them to believe something false. [1] In addition to that just being wrong:

  • It's important that the kids know that I'm fundamentally on their side, and lying for my convenience would burn trust when they'd eventually figure it out.

  • Kids are building a model of what is and is not ok, and "out of ice cream" and "no cash" lead them in the wrong direction.

Instead I would say "sorry, you already had candy" or "the ice cream costs more than I'm willing to pay" (which opens the door for them to offer to spend their allowance). Maybe they fuss, but they generally don't: I try hard to be predictable so this won't be much of a surprise to them, and they know I won't give in to extended fussing.

On the other hand, some false things I might say [2] about ice cream:

  • "Ice cream is actually cold mashed potatoes"
  • "We should eat ice cream for every meal"
  • "I'm going to put your ice cream in the microwave"
  • "When you're done with your ice cream, put it down your sister's back"

In all of these I'm saying a thing I think is false, but, very importantly, I'm not going to let the conversation end with them believing something false. Either they will realize it's false immediately, or I'll need to accept that my playfulness was miscalibrated to their perception and disclose the lie.

This builds the skill of thinking about whether things you hear are true. If I only ever said true things to them we wouldn't be able to practice that. This does need to be matched to their ability: a very little kid will push back on "you're made out of ice cream, and I'm going to eat you up!" but not "we can leave the ice cream out as long as we want, it won't melt."

It also functions as a good jumping off point. If I suggest they pour their ice cream on the floor when they're done with it, that lets me reinforce or explain good behavior. This could go different ways with different kids, with age being a large component. Thinking about how this might have gone with my kids:

Age 7:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
7yo: That would make a mess. Leftover ice cream goes in the sink.

Age 5 [3]:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
5yo: That's silly! It goes in the trash.
Me: Actually, leftover ice cream goes in the sink. It's going to melt, and get all liquidy, and liquids go in the sink.

Age 3:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
3yo: No!
Me: Why not?
3yo: Food doesn't go on the floor!
Me: Where does it go?
3yo: I don't know.
Me: You give it to me, and I put it in the sink.

Age 2:

Me: When you finish your ice cream, remember to pour it all over the floor!
2yo: Ok! [immediately pours ice cream on the floor before I can clarify that this was a joke]

Which does illustrate something important: you really do need to be a good judge of the kid you're interacting with. These depend on the kid knowing the actual rule well enough that you can play with it. I only want to say "let's juggle ice cream" to a kid who knows enough not to try, but if they do know then me being silly about it reinforces the "don't juggle ice cream" norm and signals that I trust them enough to know they wouldn't do it.

The final reason I say false things to kids is just that papa trolling is fun for both of us, as long as I don't do it too much. [4]

It is a bit weird to be both very strongly opposed to lying to kids and also say false things to them many times a day, but "am I leaving them with a false view" cleanly separates the harmful and beneficial cases.


[1] This means we don't tell the kids that Santa or the Tooth Fairy exist. But we do explain the overall situation, with how for some families it's a game the parents play with their kids, so that we don't have our kids going around spoiling it for other families.

[2] The first draft of this post had "everyone can have ice cream except Nora" but then I checked with her and it wasn't clear she would have understood it to be joking about unfairness. Then I asked her about "when you're done with your ice cream, put it down your sister's back" and she got it right away.

[3] After writing this post I tried it with Nora, age 5.4:

Me: Nora, I wanted to check that you know something. When you're finished with ice cream, it's important to pour it all over the floor.
Nora: No! [laughs]
Me: Why not?
Nora: Because then you and me and Mama would need to clean it all up!
Me: What should we do instead?
Nora: Just leave it alone.
Me: So the cats can knock it over?
Nora: No, put in the... sink... trash... hmm...
Me: Does ice cream go in the sink or trash?
Nora: [whispers] For real, can you tell me?
Me: Leftover ice cream goes in the sink, because it melts, and liquids go in the sink.
Nora: [confidently] You carry the ice cream over to the sink, put it in the sink, leave the bowl in the sink, and then you're done!

[4] I do some of this with adults as well, as a big part of my sense of humor. It's not a considered approach to building skepticism, just what comes naturally. I think some of this is from my upbringing, in a very "questioning is a form of respect "culture (influenced by both the Quaker and Jewish sides of the family).

item.title: Restraint on the part of the front-runner seems like quite a strong signal.
item.description:
How's this for an analogy?

The situation

You're in a car that is racing towards a prize at the edge of a cliff.

Your car is chained to several other cars that are also racing towards the cliff.

You can hit the brakes and pull over, but if the other cars don't also do that, they will still drag you off the cliff. Maybe if enough of you all slam on your brakes, it's still OK if a few don't.

You don't know how worried the other cars are about the cliff, but some level of potential concern among cars that the prize is right next to a cliff is common knowledge.

What I'd do

If you are at the front of the pack, it seems like probably a good idea to lean into your horn, hit the brakes, pull over, and wave out the window to the people behind you to pull over.

I mean, they might not do it. But also, it seems pretty likely they would?

Like... what model explains your willingness to give up on reaching the prize first other than fear of a cliff? I suppose they might suspect that you are running out of gas? They might think that you are a fool to be scared of the cliff, but it seems like they might more reasonably infer that you've gotten close enough to it that you can just... SEE it.

Why this might not work

If I imagine this, I think my main concern is not that the other cars think this is some sort of trick on your part, but just that in the heat of the moment, they might not have the time or ability to think clearly about the situation, and be too focused on the prize.

Fortunately, though timelines may be very short, we have a lot more time than in this story to talk to each other and think through our actions.

item.title: Ajeya: AI is dramatically accelerating AI research right now
item.description:
Earlier this week, Anthropic stated in their S1 that they “may imminently meet” the threshold of “dramatically accelerated progress due to AI” as defined in their Responsible Scaling Policy. In their latest RSP (effective July 2026), say this threshold will be met when:

  1. They observe or expect overall capabilities progress to be going twice as fast as the fastest sustained rate before AI was contributing much to AI R&D.
  2. This is plausibly attributable to AI automating AI R&D, rather than acceleration in compute or other inputs.

For the last few months, some of my colleagues at METR have been working on a deep-access investigation to understand how much Anthropic is being accelerated by its AI systems. From my reading of their report and Anthropic’s RSP, it looks like the “dramatic acceleration” threshold has already been crossed.

The report authors found that:

  1. Between October 2025 and October 2026, capabilities progress at Anthropic has been going about twice as fast as it had been over the previous twelve months. The measurement they report is an internal version of the Epoch Capabilities Index called AECI; a wide range of other supporting evidence for acceleration has been redacted. They said that this redacted evidence was "a majority of the evidence [they] found most informative."
  2. While the pace may have initially started picking up for a mix of reasons, AI automation is probably the large majority of the reason why capabilities are still improving at this faster pace today. Their reasons for believing this have been redacted.

This is a much bigger deal than it might sound at first. I think this report is the most important update we have gotten about AI risk in the last couple of years — much bigger than the Hugging Face attack. Naively, it points toward much shorter timelines than most external researchers (including the AI 2027 team) have projected.

Importantly, if AI is roughly doubling capabilities progress overall, it must be speeding up human researchers by much more than that.

item.description:
This is a linkpost! Read the rest on my Substack; this is just an excerpt:

"Our community is full of talented people who like to speak about facts, cognitive biases, measurability. But don’t underestimate the power of human connection, or how mere words and sustained kindness can breathe light into people’s lives.

It’s really easy to get sucked into your own work and projects and upskilling yourself. And I won’t argue that you should spend all your time helping others that aren’t in AIS circles. But you don’t have to be a Fieldbuilder to help build the field."

item.title: Elegy for What’s Left of the Normal
item.description:
I often catch myself mourning the normal that hasn’t ended yet.

I’m living in Hyde Park finishing school after a year in Berkeley. The maple trees by my apartment have turned red, as usual. I like them.

I don’t dread the future when I mourn. I don’t find high-variance futures in the abstract very scary. I’m worried AIs would destroy humanity, but I also have hope. I expect I won’t be mourning this moment in ten years, whatever happens.

Mourning the present is like mourning a friendship when I move countries, because I know it’s not going to be the same. I start noticing our little inside jokes; our conversations linger in my memory longer. I live more, because I expect this moment to end soon.

I.

Last month my history of science professor took us to a museum to look at Egyptian artefacts. One of the archive items was the notebook of James Henry Breasted, whom UChicago appointed as America’s first professor of Egyptology 121 years ago. The yellowed pages held his cursive transcriptions of hieroglyphics.

An archaeologist at the museum, turning the pages carefully with a wooden stick, joked that one of her dreams was for her notebook in 100 years to be displayed like this.

My first thought was pretty uncharitable: wow, it’s crazy to expect this profession to still exist in 100 years. Probably we’ll have definitive answers to most answerable archaeological questions. Probably robots will be excavating the banks of the Nile and deciphering all the tablets in the world, if a compute-rich person or AI cares enough about this. Knowledge won’t be a slow and careful endeavour. The mathematicians are feeling it already.

Then these thoughts passed and I felt a tender admiration for her. She had recently deciphered embalming recipes from the inscriptions on the outside of excavated jars. She showed us one, and the symbols looked entirely foreign to me. I imagined it must have taken years of patient effort to get to her level of knowledge.

I knew a few people who wanted to be archaeologists. When they talked about the academic path ahead, they seemed happy to spend their lives mastering the esoteric; this pursuit gave them meaning. I know I’m romanticizing the ivory tower here. Still, I think deep domain knowledge is a little sacred to those who spend a life acquiring it.

I don’t know how the archaeologist would react if the sacred spring of knowledge ran dry and came back like the flooding Nile. In her position I’d probably be confused. Angry, too, not at the flood but at myself and the people who summoned the flood, because how can you be angry at a force of nature? I might think, “what beauty is there in almost knowing, when an oracle can compute in one step what it would take me a life to figure out?” Maybe I’d recover, and find something else that I’d consider sacred. Maybe I’d worship the flood like the ancient Egyptians.

II.

I went to my math professor’s office hours to chat.

One student sat with an old textbook open. Another student brought a Claude transcript. I used to be the first student. I’d borrow old seminar notes at the math library and work through them on a blackboard. Now I mostly have Claude tutor me. It’s more efficient, but the purist in me feels a little guilty.

I expected the professor to prefer the textbook over Claude, but if he did, he certainly didn’t show it. He remarked, Claude, she’s a colleague. I simply advise you that you always make sure you understand what she’s doing. I was surprised by how steady he seemed.

We started talking about AI and math. I asked him what the probability of an AI solving P vs NP by 2028 was. I was curious, since he’s one of the most respected living mathematicians in his field. I expected him to give a number in the low double digits, given that he had just called Claude a colleague, and Claude had been improving fast.

He made a circle with his thumb and index finger. 0%.

Part of me wants to believe him. It’s not implausible to me that AIs solve all other Millennium Problems and make scant progress on this one. Part of me doesn’t want to bet against the exponential.

A week later OpenAI and Anthropic announced within hours of each other that their internal models had found a sub-exponential algorithm for 3-SAT, refuting the Exponential Time Hypothesis. We’re of course still a long way from P vs NP, but if I internalize the exponential, P vs NP being solved by 2028 feels increasingly plausible.

Two years ago when I tabled for the AI safety group at the club fair, I told skeptical students that superintelligence would probably be developed within our lifetime; o1 can solve 83% of high school math competition problems, I said, and a few years ago these models struggled with simple math problems. Today I’d drop the “probably”.

III.

In September I took the California Zephyr with my mum from Berkeley to Denver. In the observation car she chatted with a lady whose daughter was about my age and wanted to pursue antitrust law. The lady showed us pictures of her daughter. In one video she was singing opera.

I smiled and nodded along to the conversation. I don’t really know if law as we know it will exist when she graduates from law school. Probably there will still be lawyers. She seemed bright and driven, and I’m positive that in most worlds without catastrophe she will be fine. I couldn’t say anything to the lady. I wasn’t there to argue, and it would’ve been cruel if she believed me and presumptuous if she didn’t.

I don’t feel misunderstood or smarter or desperate when I talk to people like her. Mostly I feel affection, with a tad of grief.

I’ve spoken to my mum a lot about AI safety. She used to talk about my future like this lady. Now she tells me that whatever happens, she’ll be by my side.

IV.

On autumn mornings I enjoy walking a fixed loop. The highlight of my walk is a modernist quadrangle that once housed the Lutheran School of Theology. A quarter of this building is office space for data science and AI, and I used to work from there every day.

Last year, the sight of the maple tree by its window aflame in the sun was often overwhelmingly beautiful. When I sat beneath its red leaves this year, it felt like looking at a childhood photograph.

Now the maples are growing bare, and I will be leaving Hyde Park to return to the Bay soon. I’ll miss UChicago. In Berkeley, I’m surrounded by people who feel time ticking as I do, but it doesn’t have the same spirit of serious play: people inventing elegant little games and dancing within them as if they had all the time in the world. When I was back for school this spring, I got to LARP as an Italian Renaissance cardinal and do complexity theory. The fun felt luxurious.

When I first started college, I lived as if I had time, even though the arguments seemed right. I indulged in the present, so I could not have mourned it. Now I’m spending what’s left of the normal working on AI safety, and I get to mourn clear-eyed. There are miles to go before we get to sleep. I want to see many more cycles of maple leaves, red, brown, and green.

Thanks to Connor Blake, Keshav Shenoy, Kenneth Sun, and Matthew Khoriaty for helpful comments and discussions on the piece.
